5.0.0.en: 1 Now it came to pass on the third day, that Esther put on her royal apparel, and stood in the inner court of the king’s house, over against the king’s house: and the king sat upon his royal throne in the royal house, over against the gate of the house. 2 And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favour in his sight: and the king held out to Esther the golden sceptre that was in his hand. So Esther drew near, and touched the top of the sceptre.

5.0.1.en: “Now it came to pass on the third day, that Esther put on her royal apparel, and stood in the inner court of the king’s house, over against the king’s house: and the king sat upon his royal throne in the royal house, over against the gate of the house” [1].

5.0.2.en: Esther prepared herself for this meeting with fasting and humbling together with prayer, and came to meet the king on the third day to invite him with Haman to a feast that she was preparing for them. Many of the Fathers saw that the number “3” signifies the resurrection. If Esther’s feast signifies the feast of the Cross, which the Lord prepared to save His people and to crucify the devil and all his wicked works, then she went forth to this feast in the spirit of the resurrection. In other words, if this feast signifies the Cross, then the destruction that befell Haman is through the Cross of the Lord who rose from the dead. On the Cross the true Haman, that is, the devil, perished, because He who was lifted up on the Cross is “the Resurrection” Himself (Jn 11:25).

5.0.3.en: Esther went to the king as to the Cross through the power of the Lord’s resurrection; therefore she took off the sackcloth and put on royal garments, for she believed in God who raises the needy from the dunghill.

5.1.0.en: The Additions to Esther present to us a magnificent and detailed picture of Esther’s meeting with the king (Additions to Esth 15), mentioning that when she took off the garments of her mourning and put on the garments of her glory, she called upon the Governor of all and Savior of all, God [5]. It is as though she declares that for His sake she took off the sackcloth and for His sake she put on glory, and that she would not set out to the work without Him. She called upon Him to accompany her, indeed to be in her heart and speak on her tongue, indeed that she herself be hidden in Him so that He might shoot His arrows into the king’s heart to turn it from cruelty to love. She called upon God the Savior of all since she knew that “The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Prov 21:1).

5.1.1.en: Esther went with two maidservants, leaning on one as though she could not stand because of her delicateness and luxury, while the other followed her, bearing up her train... And she was radiant in color in the prime of her beauty, and her face was pleasant and very lovable. She passed through all the doors, door after door, and then stood before the king, where he was sitting on his throne in his royal attire, adorned with gold and jewels, and his appearance was terrible. He lifted up his eyes and showed the wrath of his heart by the blazing of his eyes, so the queen fell and the color of her face turned to pallor, and she leaned her head on the maidservant in faintness. But God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness, and he hastened and rose from the throne in concern and embraced her in his arms until she came to herself, and he comforted her with these words: “What is the matter, Esther? I am thy brother; be not afraid. Thou shalt not die, for the law is not for thee but for the common people. Come near and touch the sceptre.” And as she still was silent, he took the golden sceptre and laid it upon her neck and her heart, and said: “Why dost thou not speak to me?!” And she answered and said: “I saw thee, my lord, as an angel of God, and my heart was troubled for fear of thy glory. For wonderful art thou, lord, and thy countenance is full of grace.” And while she was speaking she fell again and almost fainted, and the king was troubled, and all his attendants comforted her.

5.1.2.en: It is a wonderful meeting that reveals the meeting of the living Church, hidden in Christ Jesus who rose from the dead, with the Father, that she may enjoy His love and His eternal embraces.

5.1.3.en: I say, how much we need to go forth with Esther on the third day, carrying within us the power of the Lord’s resurrection, which removes our mourning and gives us inner glories and royal garments fitting for our meeting with the heavenly Lord. Let us go forth with her, and let us also have two maidservants, leaning on the one while the other bears our train; as the Word of God took humanity as His maidservant and so appeared in the form of weakness though He is King of kings, but humanity, the other maidservant, remained behind, submitting to His divine work in harmony... Thus, with the difference, let us lean on the body as a maidservant that submits to our souls in the Lord, and let the body be behind us, walking in the steps of the Spirit and serving it, and not dominating it, moving it by its desires and temporal pleasures.

5.1.4.en: Let us walk with Esther, who appeared faint, as though she were falling under the Cross with her Christ, drinking with Him the cup of His sufferings and sharing the likeness of His death so as to bear the power of His resurrection.

5.1.5.en: Let us be like Esther, hidden in God our Savior, entering from door to door until she reaches the presence of the king. Thus the Word of God leads us in from strength to strength (Ps 84:7), and takes us from glory to glory (2 Cor 3:18), and the everlasting doors are opened before us for His sake (Ps 24:7).

5.1.6.en: Finally, when she went in to the king, he comforted her: “Esther, I am thy brother; be not afraid. Thou shalt not die, for the law is not for thee but for the common people.” Do we not hear the same words when we enter the bosom of the Father and find the Son a firstborn brother to us, interceding for us that we may enjoy fellowship in His glories, so that we do not fear judgment, for we shall not die? As the Apostle Paul says boldly: “Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us” (Rom 8:32-34).

5.1.7.en: The king embraced Esther in his arms and put the golden sceptre on her neck; thus the Father embraces us in His bosom and sets us up as a queen by the Cross (the golden sceptre), which we have received, carrying it with the Lord on our necks.

5.1.8.en: As for her saying that she saw him as an angel of God and her heart was troubled by the awe of his glory, it carries a symbol of the Church, who beholds the mysteries of God and sees His face and enters into the ecstasy of an eternal love that never ceases, and remains through all her eternity contemplating Him with love mingled with awe!

5.1.9.en: Now we repeat what St. Augustine said: [Did not God accomplish for her what she asked of Him (Additions to Esth 14:13), for He worked in the king’s heart... He heard her, and changed his heart by a hidden, effective power even before he heard her entreaties].

5.2.s.en: 2. Inviting the king and Haman to the feast:

5.2.0.en: 3 Then said the king unto her, “What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom.” 4 And Esther answered, “If it seem good unto the king, let the king and Haman come this day unto the banquet that I have prepared for him.” 5 Then the king said, “Cause Haman to make haste, that he may do as Esther hath said.” So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared. 6 And the king said unto Esther at the banquet of wine, “What is thy petition? and it shall be granted thee: and what is thy request? even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.” 7 Then answered Esther, and said, “My petition and my request is; 8 If I have found favour in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition, and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and I will do to morrow as the king hath said.”

5.2.1.en: The historian Herodotus says that the kings of Media used to refuse to let anyone enter the throne room unless he was summoned, to display their majesty and awe and at the same time to protect themselves from any assassination. As for Esther, she did not merely enter to where the throne was, but entered into the heart of the king, who embraced her in his arms and began to comfort her and ask her: “What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom!” [3]. The king did not expect Esther’s answer: “My petition and my request is; if I have found favour in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition, and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and I will do to morrow as the king hath said” [7-8].

5.3.0.en: We do not know why Esther postponed her request at a time when the king promised her that he would give her even up to half the kingdom. Did she feel some fear and want to gather her courage by prayer throughout the day? Or perhaps in her wisdom she did not want to hasten the request lest the king feel that she had pressed him and exploited his love for her?! But we know a more important explanation: she had to postpone the talk until the next day so that the cup of Haman’s wickedness might be filled and he might make the cross for Mordecai [14] so that he himself would be crucified on it. The hand of God pushed her to postpone so that God’s saving plan might be accomplished in its most wonderful form: Mordecai is glorified by Haman’s humiliation, as it was proclaimed before him in the square of the city: “Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour” (Esth 6:11), and Haman prepares the gallows for himself.

5.3.1.en: The postponement of the request was apparently by a divine revelation, if not in a tangible form then by God’s work in her heart and on her tongue, as she herself asked that He give her words of wisdom... And during this postponement God hastened to glorify Mordecai after God took sleep from the king’s eyes (Esth 6), and Haman hastened to kindle the fire to burn himself.

5.3.2.en: As for why she asked Haman to be present with the king, and this was the first time that she asked him to eat with them, as appears from Haman’s own joy and his saying to his family and friends: “Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king” [12], perhaps it is because, since she wanted to complain of him to the king, she did not accept to do so behind his back, but face to face with him. She wanted to strike two birds with one stone: to please the king by the coming of Haman, who was much beloved to him, and at the same time to accuse Haman before the king in his presence.

5.3.3.en: In any case, if this feast is the feast of the Cross that the Church holds at Golgotha, it is only to invite the King, that He may rejoice in the fruit of His suffering Church risen from the dead, and Haman attends to be condemned to the Cross and lose all his power. As St. Jerome says: [On the Cross Christ was lifted up crucified according to the flesh, but He crucified the devil and shattered his authority.

5.4.0.en: 9 Then went Haman forth that day joyful and with a glad heart: but when Haman saw Mordecai in the king’s gate, that he stood not up, nor moved for him, he was full of indignation against Mordecai. 10 Nevertheless Haman refrained himself: and when he came home, he sent and called for his friends, and Zeresh his wife. 11 And Haman told them of the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all the things wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king. 12 Haman said moreover, “Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king. 13 Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.” 14 Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, “Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet.” And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made.

5.4.1.en: “Then went Haman forth that day joyful and with a glad heart” [9], for this proud man, who thinks only of himself, counted that the queen desired to honor him by his accompanying the king at the feast, and did not know that she had invited him for his condemnation, like those who are self-admiring, deceiving themselves, as it was said to Edom: “Thou art greatly despised. The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee” (Obad 1:2-3).

5.5.0.en: He went out joyful and with a glad heart, but his joy lasted only moments, for at the gate before leaving the palace he saw Mordecai not bowing down to him, and he was filled with indignation... And so Haman gathered his household and his friends to declare to them his wealth and honor, saying: “Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate” [13]. He cannot bear to see Mordecai sitting at the king’s gate even if he himself is invited to the king’s feast. This is the mind of the devil toward the children of God, for he cannot bear any of them to sit at the gate of the King of kings, counting this a loss to him.

5.5.1.en: Let us contemplate the person of Mordecai, who offered fasts and humbling and cried bitterly in the midst of the city; we find him returning to the palace after the period of humbling, and not bowing down in prostration to Haman, for he does not accept to appease a man at the expense of the truth, nor to offer to a man what is fitting for God alone.

5.5.2.en: And since Haman had lost his peace, his wife and all his friends advised him to make a gallows fifty cubits high so that in the morning he might ask for the crucifixion of Mordecai before going in to the feast, and Haman made the gallows.

5.5.3.en: Haman made the gallows as the devil prepared the Cross through his helpers, and when Haman thought that he was crucifying Mordecai, he himself was crucified on it. So also when the devil counted that he would be rid of the Lord Christ by the Cross, the devil himself is crucified secretly, losing his authority over the Lord’s believers (Col 2:14-15).

5.5.4.en: He made a cross whose height was 50 cubits so that he might enjoy seeing Mordecai crucified while he was in the palace, from afar, and so slake his thirst for revenge. But the number 50 carries a symbolic meaning, for it signifies freedom, since in the Jubilee (the fiftieth year) the Jews granted slaves liberty, and the land was set free and returned to its owners... And by the Cross believing humanity was set free from the true Haman. For on the Cross it sees its Christ opening His arms to embrace the whole world, Jews and Gentiles, to set them free from the captivity of the devil and take them to the bosom of His Father.
